newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak GDP growth slows in 96 but still strong.
newsitem.headline: Slovak GDP growth slows in 96 but still strong.

text.p: The Slovak government said on Tuesday real economic growth, as expected, eased last year and should continue to decline in 1997, though analysts said they were surprised by the strength of the economy in 1996.
The government said in a statement that according to preliminary figures real GDP growth edged down to 6.9 percent, year-on-year, in 1996, from 7.4 percent real growth in 1995.
It added that a further gradual downtrend is expected for the first half of 1997, with real growth easing to 5.7 percent from real growth of 7.1 percent in the first half of 1996.
"Slovakia's economy continued to grow in 1996 and preliminary figures show real GDP growth of 6.9 percent," a statement issued at a regular government meeting said.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) had forecast GDP growth for the whole of 1996 at 7.0 percent.
The government statement added that SUSR expected average annual inflation was seen at 6.0 percent by the end of the first half of the year.
Analysts said the 1996 figure was surprisingly strong given a region-wide economic downturn last year and the central bank's tight monetary policy.

"We know the economy has been quite strong, there have been signs of overheating, but it appears to have exceeded expectations," said Jonathan Garner, an economist at Robert Fleming Securities in London.
"We have only seen a few of the figures and no real breakdown, but we were expecting growth closer to around the 5.5-6.0 percent level," he added.
The only other figure released by the government concerning GDP in 1996 was that it totalled 581.3 billion crowns.
The central bank implemented a series of measures last July aiming to tighten the money supply and curb inflation and the expansion of credit.
The moves included hikes in the last-resort lending facility, the Lombard rate and minimum reserve requirements for banks, as well as a measure aimed at curbing domestic lending.
It then further moved to reduce loan expansion at the beginning of 1997, setting new rules for foreign exchange positions for monetary purposes -- and penalties for breaching the measures.
Last week, the NBS said it was still waiting to see the impact of its moves to rein in credit expansion, though it added that it was prepared to act to support its foreign exchange reserves.
